children: AI ANGST DOESN'T HAVE TO MEAN THE END OF THE AI TRADE
Artificial intelligence has advanced so quickly that even the people building it are urging caution, according to Blake Anderson, director, portfolio management at Carson Group.

In recent weeks, leaders at OpenAI and Anthropic have warned that cutting-edge AI systems are evolving faster than expected. As AI moves beyond chatbots toward more autonomous agents, researchers say the technology is becoming harder to fully understand and predict. In a note published Monday, Anderson highlighted that even frontier researchers have expressed surprise at some of the capabilities emerging from these systems.

Those warnings have contributed to investor unease, particularly in technology and semiconductor stocks. Many AI-linked names have pulled back sharply from their summer highs as traders weigh whether safety concerns could slow the pace of development. Still, Anderson argues that caution does not necessarily weaken the long-term AI story.

In his view, today's concerns could ultimately strengthen the technology by encouraging better safeguards and oversight. Anderson points to chain-of-thought monitoring as one promising development. The approach aims to give researchers greater visibility into how AI systems arrive at decisions before they act, helping improve understanding and potentially reduce unintended consequences.

Technology breakthroughs have always brought both opportunity and risk, Anderson says, and AI appears no different. While recent warnings have highlighted the challenges posed by increasingly powerful systems, they have also spurred efforts to better understand and manage them. If researchers can improve transparency and control without stalling innovation, Anderson believes today's AI angst could eventually give way to a broader appreciation of AI's long-term potential.
